quizName: Lab 3: A Tour of git Commands

questions.question: Why should `lab03-exercises` be a sibling of `class-exercises-fall2026` (both under `csci338`), not inside it?
options: Nested git repositories cause problems; each repo should have its own top-level folder
GitHub only allows one folder per account
So you can skip creating a README
questions.explanation: A git repo should not live inside another git repo. Keep `lab03-exercises` next to `class-exercises-fall2026`, not nested under it.

questions.question: You create `README.md` and run `git add README.md` before `git init`. What goes wrong?
options: Git has no repository yet, so you get an error until you run `git init`
questions.explanation: `git add` and `git commit` only work inside a repository. `git init` creates the `.git` directory that makes the folder a repo.

questions.question: After `git init`, what new hidden item appears in the directory?
questions.explanation: `git init` creates `.git`, which stores commits, branches, and other repository state. You usually do not edit it by hand.

questions.question: What are you mainly checking for when you run `git status`?
options: The contents of every commit ever made
Which branch you are on, and which files are untracked / staged / modified
questions.explanation: `git status` shows the current branch and the working-tree state (untracked files, staged changes, etc.). Get in the habit of checking it often.

questions.question: What does `git add README.md` do?
options: Puts the file in the staging area for the next commit
questions.explanation: Staging (`git add`) selects what will be included in the next `git commit`. It does not upload anything by itself.

questions.question: After you edit a tracked file, which command shows the line-by-line changes since the last commit?
questions.explanation: `git diff` shows unstaged changes in the working tree compared to what was last committed (or staged, depending on flags).

questions.question: In Git terms, what is a **remote** (like `origin`)?
options: A temporary stash of uncommitted edits
A copy of the repository living somewhere else (often on GitHub)
The same thing as a branch
questions.explanation: Git is distributed: your laptop has a full copy, and GitHub holds another copy. By convention that GitHub copy is named `origin`.

questions.question: For collaborative / production work, why avoid committing directly to `main`?
options: Because `git push` only works on feature branches
So changes can go through a branch + pull request process (review, checks) before landing on `main`
questions.explanation: Treat `main` as sacred. Commit on a feature branch, open a PR, then merge so process (tests, review) can protect `main`.

questions.question: You run `git branch more-tests` while on `main`. What is true afterward?
options: `more-tests` is created if it doesn't exist, but you are still on `main` until you `checkout` (or switch to) it
The branch is already on GitHub
questions.explanation: `git branch <name>` creates a branch but does not switch to it. The `*` in `git branch` marks your current branch; use `git checkout more-tests` (or `git switch`) to move.

questions.question: You commit on `more-tests`, then `git checkout main`. What happens to your working tree?
options: Files update to match `main`'s latest commit; `more-tests`'s commits are still saved on that branch
Nothing — every branch always shows the same files
questions.explanation: Checking out a branch updates your files to that branch's tip. Other branches keep their history; switch back to see those commits again.

questions.question: What does `git diff main..more-tests` show?
options: The differences between the tips of `main` and `more-tests`
questions.explanation: That form of `git diff` compares two branches so you can see what would change if you brought `more-tests` into `main`.

questions.question: After a PR is merged on GitHub, your local repo does not update by itself. Which pair of ideas matches the lab?
options: `git init` downloads remote commits; `git add` applies them
`git commit` syncs with GitHub; `git status` pushes
`git fetch` downloads remote updates without merging; `git pull` brings them into your current branch
questions.explanation: Merging on GitHub changes the remote. Locally, `fetch` updates remote-tracking refs; `pull` integrates those changes into your current branch (often `main`).

questions.question: What does `git branch -D more-tests` do?
options: Deletes the remote repository on GitHub
Deletes the local branch `more-tests` after you no longer need it
questions.explanation: After the PR is merged and you have updated local `main`, you can delete the finished local feature branch with `git branch -D`.

questions.question: Which statement best describes Git vs GitHub?
options: Git is the version-control system; GitHub is a hosting/collaboration platform built around Git
They are the same tool with two names
Git only works offline; GitHub only works without git
questions.explanation: You use git commands locally. GitHub stores remotes, PRs, issues, and related collaboration features.

questions.question: In Git, what is the **working tree** (working directory)?
options: Only the remote copy of the repo on GitHub
The project files on disk that you edit — the checkout of the commit you are on, plus any uncommitted changes
A list of all branch names forever
questions.explanation: The working tree is what you see in your folder: the files for the current commit, plus edits that are not committed yet. `git status` reports how that tree differs from the last commit / staging area.

questions.question: From Git's point of view, what is a **branch**?
options: A named pointer to a commit (usually the tip of a line of work); moving the pointer does not erase other commits
A full second copy of every file on disk
questions.explanation: A branch is a lightweight name that points at a commit. New commits on that branch advance the pointer. Other branches keep their own pointers to their tips.

questions.question: From a data-structure perspective, what is a **commit**?
options: Only a commit message string with no link to files
A random folder Git creates outside your project
A snapshot of the project (a tree of files) plus metadata, linked to its parent commit(s) — so history forms a directed acyclic graph (DAG)
questions.explanation: Each commit records a tree (file snapshot), author/message/time, and parent pointer(s). Commits chain into a DAG; merges have more than one parent.

questions.question: In Git, what is **HEAD**?
options: A pointer to your current location — usually the tip of the branch you have checked out (where the next commit will go)
questions.explanation: HEAD is where you are right now. On a normal branch checkout, HEAD points at that branch name, and the branch points at a commit. Detached HEAD means HEAD points straight at a commit instead of a branch.
